content: CD9 antigen is a protein encoded by the CD9 gene in humans. This protein belongs to the transmembrane 4 superfamily, also referred to as the tetraspanin family. Proteins in this family are typically cell-surface proteins characterized by the presence of four hydrophobic domains. These proteins are involved in signal transduction processes that regulate various cellular functions, including development, activation, growth, and motility. CD9 is a cell surface glycoprotein that forms complexes with integrins and other members of the transmembrane 4 superfamily. It is present on the surface of exosomes and plays a role in modulating cell adhesion and migration. Additionally, CD9 is capable of triggering platelet activation and aggregation. This protein also facilitates muscle cell fusion and contributes to the maintenance of myotubes. CD9 is critically involved in the process of egg-sperm fusion during mammalian fertilization. While oocytes are ovulated, those deficient in CD9 fail to properly fuse with sperm during fertilization. CD9 is localized in the microvillar membrane of oocytes and appears to play a role in maintaining the normal morphology of oocyte microvilli. CD9 has been shown to interact with several other proteins, including CD117, CD29, CD46, CD49c, CD81, PTGFRN, and TSPAN4.
